column2: P6 and Power BI Report Server
column4: This video explains how our business platform connects to Power BI Report Server. Users keep their existing accounts and open reports inside the platform. Administrators manage access and row-level security from the same application. We will follow the login process, show the demo screens, and explain where each permission is enforced.

PBIRS is short for Power BI Report Server. Authors create reports in Desktop and publish them to the server. PBIRS stores the reports and models, runs queries, and renders the visuals. Our platform handles users, navigation, and permission management. This lets us reuse the reporting engine instead of building another one.

There are two main routes. Windows integrated authentication uses Active Directory accounts. Custom authentication uses accounts from our own application. Because our platform already manages users, the Active Directory route would require synchronizing two account systems. We chose custom authentication so that a new application user does not also need a domain account.

In the test environment, the demo application and PBIRS run on the same machine as separate services. The demo backend provides account verification, identity tickets, and permission APIs. PBIRS loads our security extension and custom login page. A stable user identifier connects the two systems. Report requests use the actual user, rather than a shared Windows administrator identity.

column2: From application login to report access
column4: After the user signs in, the backend issues a short-lived identity ticket. PBIRS verifies its signature and expiry and prevents replay. It then creates a reporting session for that user. Later report requests reuse this session, so no second password prompt is needed. Single sign-on shares the identity, while each system still maintains its own session.

Opening PBIRS directly leads to our custom login page, deployed under ReportServer. The page calls the demo authentication service on the server side. Once the account is verified, it creates a PBIRS session and returns to the portal. We replaced the login entry point while retaining the existing report portal and reporting engine.

This is our user management page. Administrators can create accounts, reset passwords, and activate or deactivate users. A new account has no report permissions until access is assigned. Demo administration and PBIRS portal administration are separate responsibilities. The English interface shown here is a video preview; the deployed demo currently supports Chinese and Portuguese.

column2: Embedding a report in the platform
column4: The outer page provides navigation, folders, and search. An iframe opens the PBIRS report viewer inside it. Filtering, visual interaction, and data queries still run through the report server. A business dashboard can be designed as a single report page. PBIRS does not provide the native Dashboard object from the cloud Power BI service.

Permissions have two layers. Resource permissions decide whether a user can open a folder or report. Row-level security, or RLS, decides which records that user can see inside the report. For example, someone may open a contributions report but see only their assigned region. Assigning an RLS model role does not automatically grant permission to open the report.

The administrator selects a user and checks folders or individual reports. The backend writes the selections to PBIRS, so direct report links are checked as well. Users also need browsing permission on the ancestor folders. The current test implementation reconciles permissions periodically. A production publishing process must also address the inheritance window for newly created resources.

RLS rules belong to the report model. The author creates roles, defines table filters, and publishes them with the report. For example, the Region A role can allow only records whose Province value is A. Many users can share one model role. Our demo reads existing roles and manages user assignments; it does not edit the filter expressions.

Select a user to load model roles from every report. Existing assignments are checked automatically. The administrator can change roles across reports and save once. The backend updates only changed reports, preserves other users, and reads the assignments back. PBIRS has no cross-report transaction, so the page shows individual failures rather than declaring the entire batch successful.

The test report contains six synthetic records. Demo one sees the three Region A records, totaling six hundred. Demo two sees Region B, totaling fifteen hundred. Demo three has both roles and sees all six records, totaling twenty-one hundred. Changing the role changes query results. Removing every role denies the query. This verifies model security, not a visual filter.

A future extension can map a business role to model roles across reports. The backend expands the business role into individual users. When membership or mappings change, it recalculates effective access and writes user assignments to PBIRS. Permissions from multiple sources must be combined before revoking access. This synchronizes assignments, not report data. Automatic business-role expansion is not implemented yet.

We added a security extension and login page, configured custom authentication, and connected the application account service. Folder access and model-role members are managed through APIs. The original portal, reporting engine, and RLS query behavior remain in use. We did not modify FullTrust configuration. Production integration can reuse this connection and add business roles, auditing, and deployment controls.
